There is a genuine conflict in the evidence on whether longer website content ranks better on Google. Several studies and sources argue in favor of longer content: [d1] reports that the average content length for pages ranking in Google's top ten is at least 2,000 words, with the #1 result averaging 2,416 words, and [d11] corroborates this with similar figures. [d10] (Semrush, analyzing 28,000 domains) found that "content ranking in the top positions was on average 3.5 times longer than other lower-ranking pieces," and [d6] (HubSpot) states that "long content typically ranks better" due to greater dwell time, which it calls an important ranking factor. [d2] similarly notes that "longer is generally better" and that posts in the first 10 Google positions average 1,890 words, while [d7] cites studies showing posts over 1,500 words earn significantly more backlinks and social shares, indirectly boosting rankings.

However, other credible sources directly challenge this view. [d4] (Smart Insights) cites Google's Webmaster Trends Analyst John Mueller, who stated in August 2019 that "word count is not a ranking factor," and notes that Google Quality Raters do not even count every word. [d8] (Ahrefs) found only a moderate positive correlation between length and traffic up to 2,000 words, but a moderate *negative* correlation beyond that threshold — meaning the average 10,000-word post gets less traffic than the average 2,000-word post — and also references Mueller's same statement.
